tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

type.description: What kind of feedback this is.

title.description: Short, specific one-line summary of the issue.

details.description: Labeled bullets, in order: **What happened:** (observed vs. expected, exact error text if short); **What the user said:** (quoted, or "User didn't comment; observed by the model."); **Repro:** (minimal steps); **Evidence:** (request IDs, timestamps, paths, versions; omit if none); optionally a final **Cause:** only if verified in-session. One to three lines per bullet. No narrative paragraphs, no speculation, no secrets.

area.description: Optional short tag naming the part of Claude Code this is about (e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing"). Leave blank if unclear.

failure_mode.description: When the report is about MODEL BEHAVIOR (not a product bug), the closest failure mode, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value. Omit only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.

task_category.description: What kind of task the session was doing when the issue occurred, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

A workflow size guideline is configured for this session: medium — keep workflows under 10 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale.

script.description: Self-contained workflow script. Must begin with `export const meta = { name, description, phases }` (pure literal, no computed values) followed by the script body using agent()/parallel()/pipeline()/phase().

name.description: Name of a predefined workflow (built-in or from .claude/workflows/). Resolves to a self-contained script.

description.description: Ignored — set the workflow description in the script's `meta` block.

title.description: Ignored — set the workflow title in the script's `meta` block.

args.description: Optional input value exposed to the script as the global `args`, verbatim. Pass arrays/objects as actual JSON values, NOT as a JSON-encoded string — a stringified list breaks `args.filter`/`args.map` in the script. Use for parameterized named workflows (e.g. a research question).

scriptPath.description: Path to a workflow script file on disk. Every Workflow invocation persists its script under the session directory and returns the path in the tool result. To iterate, edit that file with Write/Edit and re-invoke Workflow with the same `scriptPath` instead of re-sending the full script. Takes precedence over `script` and `name`.

resumeFromRunId.description: Run ID of a prior Workflow invocation to resume from. Completed agent() calls with unchanged (prompt, opts) return their cached results instantly; only edited or new calls re-run. Same-session only. Stop the prior run first (TaskStop) before resuming.

content.content:
Fireflies CLI — Every Fireflies meeting feature, plus offline search, cross-meeting intelligence, and a local database no other tool ha…

Highlights (not in the official API docs):
  • transcripts search   Full-text search across all synced meeting transcripts without consuming any API quota.
  • person timeline   Chronological meeting history with a specific person — topics, action items, and talk ratio per meeting.
  • action-items list   Aggregate action items from all meetings in a date range — weekly commitment audit in one command.
  • transcripts find   Find meetings by participant email, channel name, keyword, or date range — all client-side, no broken API date filters.
  • transcripts status   Show PROCESSED / PROCESSING / FAILED status for recent meetings upfront — know before you fetch.
  • topics list   Most frequent topics across all meetings in a date range — what is actually consuming meeting time.
  • digest   Aggregate view of all recent meetings: titles, gists, topics, and action items in one structured output.
  • transcripts export   Export a transcript as markdown to a vault directory with auto-generated YYYY-MM-DD_title.md filename.

Agent mode: add --agent to any command for JSON output + non-interactive mode.
Health check: run 'fireflies-pp-cli doctor' to verify auth and connectivity.
See README.md or the bundled SKILL.md for recipes.

Usage:
  fireflies-pp-cli [command]

Available Commands:
  action-items  Extract action items from transcripts
  agent-context Emit structured JSON describing this CLI for agents
  analytics     Query meeting analytics
  api           Browse all API endpoints by interface name
  auth          Manage authentication for Fireflies
  channels      Get a single channel
  completion    Generate the autocompletion script for the specified shell
  digest        Aggregate summary of recent meetings — titles, decisions, and action items
  doctor        Check CLI health
  feedback      Record feedback about this CLI (local by default; upstream opt-in)
Manage Fireflies transcripts. Run 'sync' first to populate the local store.

Usage:
  fireflies-pp-cli transcripts [command]

Available Commands:
  delete      Delete a transcript from Fireflies
  export      Export a transcript as markdown to a file or vault path
  find        Find transcripts by participant, channel, keyword, or date range
  get         Get a transcript from local store (or API with --live)
  list        List transcripts from local store
  pull        Fetch full transcript (sentences + analytics) from API and store locally
  recent      Show recently processed transcripts
  search      Full-text search across synced transcript titles and summaries
  share       Share a transcript with external email addresses
  status      Show processing status of recent meetings (PROCESSED / PROCESSING / FAILED)
  update      Update transcript title or privacy

Flags:
  -h, --help   help for transcripts

Global Flags:
      --agent                Set all agent-friendly defaults (--json --compact --no-input --no-color --yes)
      --compact              Return only key fields (id, name, status, timestamps) for minimal token usage
      --config string        Config file path
      --csv                  Output as CSV (table and array responses)
      --data-source string   Data source for read commands: auto (live with local fallback), live (API only), local (synced data only) (default "auto")
      --deliver string       Route output to a sink: stdout (default), file:<path>, webhook:<url>
      --dry-run              Show request without sending
      --human-friendly       Enable colored output and rich formatting

1	# Plan: Performance Technology Best Practices (NCAA SSI)
2	
3	Draft 2026-10-04 (recipient changed from Chris Ruf to Kenny Boyd 2026-10-07), for agreement with Kenny Boyd by **2026-10-14** (charter step 1).
4	Source material and the full gap analysis: `docs/SOURCES.md`.
5	
6	## What this document is
7	
8	A Baylor best-practices document that puts the NCAA SSI *Performance Technologies
9	Recommendations: Responsible Use in Collegiate Athletics* (CSMAS/SSI, March 2026) into
10	practice in four areas Kenny signs off on:
11	
12	1. Technology adoption plan
13	2. Athlete consent
14	3. Vendor data contracts
15	4. Staff-transition continuity
16	
17	**Done means:** Kenny signs it off, and it is in use by 2026-12-16.
18	
19	## Three decisions to get from Kenny first
20	
21	Everything below assumes the recommendation in each. If he picks the other option,
22	the outline changes, but the schedule doesn't.
23	
24	| # | Decision | Recommendation | Why |
25	|---|---|---|---|
26	| 1 | Best-practice guide or formal department policy? | **Guide plus procedures and forms**, with a one-page policy statement only if Kenny wants one | At the 2026-07-30 meeting, leadership preferred "flexible best-practice documents over rigid formal policy". UT chose formal policy (SMED-8055); we can follow its structure without its formality. |
27	| 2 | How does this relate to the Software & Technology Management Framework (draft, 08-14)? | **This document is the framework's "Version 1" content.** The framework keeps the request and review process (SSI Rec 4). This document supplies what the framework marks "planned for Version 1": the working group, consent, education, the transfer protocol, the feedback loop | Avoids two documents covering the same process. The framework's request process is already built. |
28	| 3 | Scope: only the four areas, or the four plus education? | **Four areas plus a short education section** | SSI calls education "foundational for informed consent" (Rec 2), so consent can't stand without it. Keep education to who, how often and what topics, not a curriculum. |
29	
30	## Proposed outline of the document
31	
32	0. **Purpose and scope.** SSI basis, definitions (SSI's own, as UT does), who it applies to.
33	1. **Governance.** A standing Performance Technology Working Group: multidisciplinary, with student-athlete members (SSI Rec 1.1). Annual review of this document. Named owner. Medical authority over return-to-play stays with Athletic Medicine (Rec 3.3).
34	2. **Technology adoption.** Points to the framework's request and review process (Rec 4). Adds only what it lacks: the "start from the question" rule (Iowa State's intake form), and one scoring instrument. Today the March checklist and the framework scorecard compete; reconcile them into one.
35	3. **Athlete consent and education.**
36	   - Notice versus consent: which data needs opt-in consent, and which is unavoidable but disclosed. Webinar line: venue tracking is unavoidable, a wearable needs consent.
37	   - Consent form, built from the March template: voluntary, withdraw without penalty, retention, transfer.
38	   - Disclosure when de-identified data goes to vendor norm-building.
39	   - Annual re-consent, and re-consent when a new technology is introduced.
40	   - Where consent records live.
41	   - Annual education by group (Rec 2.1–2.3).
42	4. **Data management.**
43	   - Ownership, storage, access, and who may interpret and communicate data (Rec 3, 3.1).
44	   - The physiologic versus performance data classification.
45	   - Collect only what is used ("if you're not doing anything with it, don't collect it").
46	   - Transfer-athlete protocol (Rec 3.2).
47	5. **Vendor data contracts.**
48	   - A standard data addendum or clause checklist: ownership, permitted use, storage and jurisdiction, AI training, downstream sharing, data-for-discount or norm-pooling terms, retention and deletion, portability, breach notification.
49	   - **An exit clause:** return or delete data when a product is dropped. Nothing does this today.
50	   - An audit of existing contracts (about 50 vendors), run with Legal and Procurement.
51	6. **Staff-transition continuity** (no SSI or framework source; original work).
52	   - Every platform has a named institutional admin account, never a personal one.
53	   - Access removal on departure, with a checklist and a timeline.
54	   - A data custodian per platform, with a backup.
55	   - A handover note for each system the person ran.
56	   - Vendor contact and renewal dates recorded in the tech inventory.
57	7. **Continuous improvement.** An annual student-athlete feedback survey (Rec 5.2), staff feedback (5.3), and a working-group review that revises this document (5.1).
58	- **Appendices (forms):** consent form, vendor data addendum checklist, offboarding checklist, annual review checklist.
59	
60	Target length: the guide in about 8–10 pages, with forms separate. Format: Baylor_Doc_Style (docx + pdf).
61	
62	## Schedule (charter dates in bold)
63	
64	| When | Step | Output |
65	|---|---|---|
66	| By **10/14** | Meet Kenny, settle decisions 1–3 and agree this plan | Charter step 1 done |
67	| 10/15–10/24 | Inputs: Legal/OGC (ownership, HIPAA/FERPA/Texas classification, consent model), Procurement (contract list, addendum), ITS (offboarding, admin accounts), Athletic Medicine (medical authority, physiologic data). Follow up the May outside-counsel proposal | Answers to the open questions; contract list |
68	| 10/20–11/05 | Draft sections 0–7, reusing the March drafts and the framework text | Draft v1 |
69	| By **11/06** | First draft to Kenny | Charter step 2 |
70	| 11/09–11/20 | Revise; review the consent form with OGC; review the offboarding checklist with ITS | Draft v2 |
71	| By **11/25** | Final delivered | Charter step 3 |
72	| By **12/16** | In use: Kenny signs off and the guide is posted where staff can find it (decided 2026-10-05, `docs/ssi-open-decisions-design.md` D5) | Charter step 4 |
73	
74	## Who needs to be involved
75	
76	- **Kenny Boyd:** receiver and sign-off.
77	- **Athletic Medicine:** medical authority, physiologic data.
78	- **OGC/Legal:** ownership, consent, contracts.
79	- **Procurement / Business Office:** vendor contracts.
80	- **ITS:** storage, security, offboarding.
81	- **Compliance:** education sessions, NIL.
82	- **Student-athlete voice:** SAAC or similar, for the working group and feedback.
83	
84	## Risks
85	
86	- **Legal answers arrive late.** Draft with the March positions marked "pending OGC", so legal review slots in without blocking the draft.
87	- **The framework draft is parked** (archived repo, "Draft for discussion"). If Kenny won't treat it as live, section 2 has to carry the adoption process itself, which means more writing in that section.
88	- **Contract audit scale** (about 50 vendors). Plan the audit process and a priority list (wearables and force plates first), not the full audit, inside this deadline.
89	
90	## Questions for the Kenny meeting (short list)
91	
92	1. Decisions 1–3 above.
93	2. Who owns the document and signs it (UT uses its Chief Medical Officer)?
94	3. Data ownership position: institution-owned with athlete access (the March draft), or athlete-owned for physiologic data (the framework spec's posture)?
95	4. Who can we go to in OGC, Procurement and ITS, and did the May outside-counsel proposal go anywhere?
96	5. Does a working group with student-athlete members get chartered, and can education ride on existing compliance and orientation sessions?

1	BAYLOR ATHLETICS  ·  APPLIED PERFORMANCE
2	Software and Technology Management Framework
3	A three-phase process for requesting, approving, implementing, and reviewing software and technology across Baylor Athletics.
4	1. Purpose
5	To increase the efficiency and transparency of requests for software and technology, ensuring staff feel assured of fair decision-making.
6	2. Scope and terminology
7	“Software and technology” is used deliberately as a single term. Technology refers to tangible items — devices, wearables, equipment and applications. Software refers to the platforms and systems those items connect to. The two are rarely purchased independently, and this framework covers both.
8	The framework is department-wide. It is not limited to performance, health and wellness, or any single unit — a request from fan engagement follows the same path as a request from football.
9	3. Why now — alignment with NCAA guidance and compliance requirements to ensure the process meets external standards and mitigates risks.
10	The NCAA Sports Science Institute has published guidance on the Responsible Use of Performance Technologies in College Athletics. That guidance is high-level by design, leaving each school to implement it according to its own needs and resources. This framework is Baylor Athletics' implementation.
11	Framing note: the intent is alignment and collective effort, not to imply current practice is deficient. This fosters trust and shared responsibility among staff.
12	4. Intended outcomes
13	A consistent, shared understanding of the entire inventory of software and technology in use across the department.
14	Improved utilization of what the department already owns, surfaced by the Phase 3 usage review.
15	Coordinated renewal and term review, so the department stops discovering it is in the final year of an agreement with no time to act.
16	Increased staff fluency — so sport administrators and unit staff can speak to technology questions rather than defaulting to whatever is asked for in the moment.
17	5. Roles
18	6. The three phases
19	Phase 1 — Proposal, Approval, Purchase
20	1.1  A request is initiated by the Director of Applied Performance, a Head Coach, or an Admin Unit Director.
21	1.2  The requester completes the Technology Idea Form and the internal ATH Form. The request must declare its data category and proposed review tier.
22	1.3  The request goes to the Business Office. The Business Office is the filter for all requests and is the first control point — no request proceeds without clearing it.
23	1.4  The forms are submitted to ITS for technical, security, and integration review. This is the second control point.
24	1.5  The request is evaluated against the Technology Evaluation Scorecard at a depth set by its tier (Section 7).
25	1.6  A request is disseminated for purchase only after clearing both control points. Declined requests are returned with documented reasons.
26	1.7  The DAPP holds a weekly standing meeting with the ITS representative to review the status of all open requests across all units.
27	Phase 2 — Implementation and Product Use
28	2.1  A project manager is assigned. This may be administrative staff other than the DAPP, depending on the unit and the system.
29	2.2  Status flows from the weekly ITS standing meeting through the DAPP to the assigned project manager and stakeholders, so that every open request has a known owner and a known blocker.
30	2.3  Open requests are tracked on the shared request tracker: project, item, requester, project manager, date submitted, desired implementation date, current status, and what is holding it up.
31	Phase 3 — Product Review and Renewal Decision
32	3.1  Review is triggered at six months, or at the end of the competitive season — whichever is longer. Tools used primarily in season are therefore judged on in-season usage.
33	3.2  The review compares actual utilization against the intent stated on the original request.
34	3.3  Low utilization opens a diagnostic conversation before a renewal conclusion. A tool may be under-used because the vendor is failing, the integration is broken, or training never happened — each has a different remedy, and only one of them is cancellation.
35	3.4  The outcome is renew, modify or renegotiate, or discontinue. The decision and its rationale feed the software inventory and the term/renewal calendar.
36	7. Review depth scales to risk
37	Not every request warrants the same scrutiny. Applying a full evaluation to a single-team, low-cost tool with no athlete data would create work without reducing risk. Three tiers:
38	Dollar thresholds separating the tiers are deliberately left blank — that is a Business Office decision (Appendix B).
39	8. Exceptions
40	8.1  Urgent and “emergency” requests
41	An expedited lane, not a bypass. Urgent requests clear the same control points on a compressed clock, with a short risk checklist completed at intake to surface issues that would otherwise delay the request: data category, contract term, integration dependency, and whether athlete data leaves Baylor.
42	This should be stated plainly: most urgent requests are reactive — something has happened, and the technology is needed now. No procurement process delivers on that timeline. The framework's real answer to urgency is to make routine requests predictable enough, and planning far enough ahead, that fewer requests become emergencies.
43	8.2  Product trials and pilots
44	Trials run under provisional approval in a contained environment:
45	A defined start and hard end date, agreed at approval.
46	No physiologic data and no identifiable athlete data until full approval.
47	A named owner and a stated question the trial is meant to answer.
48	A mandatory review at the end of the trial that converts to full approval or terminates. A trial that continues has become a purchase without a decision.
49	9. Workflow
50	Appendix A  ·  Data categorization, ownership and protection
51	A1.  How are we categorizing data?
52	Before ownership can be determined, data has to be sorted into buckets. Three categories, distinguished by who generates the data and whether it is internal or external to the athlete:
53	A further distinction applies within performance data: individual versus team. Team data is aggregated from individual data and treated as such.
54	A2.  Who owns the data?
55	The prevailing position, and the one most commonly stated across the industry, is that data generated by the athlete belongs to the athlete and is held under institutional stewardship. Business operations data is institutional. The boundary is genuinely contestable at the margins — athletes generate a third-down conversion rate, but it is plainly institutional — which is precisely why the categories in A1 matter more than a single ownership statement.
56	A3.  Does consent work the same way for every category?
57	Recommendation for discussion. Performance data may reasonably be covered by a blanket consent obtained at onboarding. Physiologic data may warrant consent tied to a specific use and a specific time, rather than a blanket permission — recording what was consented to, for what purpose, and when. The mechanism and system of record for this do not currently exist and would need to be built.
58	A4.  Who should be able to see raw physiologic data?
59	Recommendation for discussion. Two related proposals:
60	No single individual should be the sole holder of athletes' physiologic data, and medical staff should be part of the routing path.
61	Coaching staff may be better served by summary output than by raw physiologic data — the precedent already exists in how DEXA and body composition results are handled today.
62	Framing matters here, and this will not be universally welcomed. The intent is to unburden coaches from information that will not change their decisions and to let the specialist own the interpretation — not to withhold. Where that framing fails, the underlying issue is usually trust between staff groups, which a policy document cannot resolve on its own.
63	A5.  What happens when someone outside Baylor needs access?
64	External consultants and contractors working with student-athlete data require an executed agreement carrying institutional privacy and data protection terms before access is granted — beyond the standard outside-consultant agreement handled through compliance. This is already current practice and should be stated in the framework so it is applied consistently rather than on a case-by-case basis.
65	Sharing an individual athlete's data externally — for example, providing performance numbers to a professional scout — requires that athlete's consent.
66	A6.  What legal considerations sit behind this?
67	Flagged for legal review, not offered as legal advice:
68	FERPA protects student records and may impose consent, retention and disclosure obligations when records are released to third parties — including AI vendors that analyze athlete data.
69	HIPAA governs the use, security, and disclosure of protected health information when tools access medical and injury records.
70	State privacy laws increasingly scrutinize wearable-derived data such as heart rate, sleep, and stress indicators.
71	The practical consequence of this framework is that the data category declared at intake determines which of these are in play, which is why the declaration sits on the request form rather than being discovered later.
72	A7.  What must a request declare about data?
73	Every request declares: the data category; whether data leaves Baylor systems; who receives and interfaces with the output; where the data is stored; and what happens to it at end of term. These determine the review tier, route the request to the correct reviewers, and let ITS reach a yes-or-no decision faster.
74	Appendix B  ·  Open decisions for the group
75	These belong to the stakeholder group, not to Applied Performance. They are the deliberate 20% left open in this draft.
76	Appendix C  ·  Source materials
77	NCAA Sports Science Institute — guidance on the Responsible Use of Performance Technologies in College Athletics.
78	Eversheds Sutherland — “How to get ahead? Harnessing athlete performance data” (summarises the NCAA guidance and the FERPA / HIPAA / state-law considerations above).
79	Sports Tech Research Network — Quality Framework for Sports Technologies (white paper, assessment sheet, and “Bringing the Framework to Life”, v1.0 December 2024). Basis for the evaluation scorecard.
80	Baylor Applied Performance — Sports Tech Evaluation Assessment Sheet (2024), the existing internal adaptation of the STRN framework.
81	Status | DRAFT v0.9 — for discussion, 2026-08-10
82	Prepared by | Eric Rash, Director of Applied Performance
83	Requested by | Kenny Boyd
84	For review | Monday 10 August 2026
85	Purpose of draft | 80% draft. Decisions reserved for the stakeholder group are marked throughout and collected in Appendix B.
86	How to read this draft
87	This document is intentionally unfinished. The process in Sections 4–7 is proposed for adoption, with input from legal, compliance, and medical teams to ensure comprehensive review and address concerns.
88	NCAA SSI recommendation | Where this framework addresses it
89	Implement written policies that establish standards and procedures and increase transparency. | This document
90	Educate student-athletes so that consent is informed | Appendix A — consent and categorization
91	Manage data rights — ownership, storage, access authority, permitted use | Appendix A; Ownership and Privacy gate features on the scorecard
92	Establish a process for implementing new technologies, applied consistently and cross-disciplinarily | Phase 1 — Proposal, Approval, Purchase
93	Develop a system for continual improvement | Phase 3 — Product Review and Renewal Decision
94	Role | Responsibility in this framework
95	Requesting party
96	(Head Coach, Admin Unit Director, or DAPP) | Initiates the request. Completes the Idea Form and internal ATH Form, including the data category declaration.
97	Business Office | First control point. Filters ALL requests before they proceed — budget, contract, and duplication check.
98	ITS | Second control point. Technical, security, and integration review; confirms the system can be supported.
99	Director of Applied Performance (DAPP) | Single point of contact and facilitator. Holds the weekly standing meeting with ITS and relays status to project managers and stakeholders.
100	Assigned Project Manager | Owns delivery of the individual project. May be administrative staff other than DAPP.
101	Sport Administrator | Signs off on renewal decisions at Phase 3, informed by the usage review.
102	Health & Wellness / Medical | Reviews requests involving physiologic or health data (Elevated tier).
103	What the DAPP role is not
104	The Director of Applied Performance is the single point of contact — not the subject-matter expert for every system, and not the project manager for every project. The role is to keep requests visible and moving, and to make sure the right people are in the conversation. Delivery accountability stays with the assigned project manager and the requesting unit.
105	Why the review matters
106	The review is what gives sign-off authority something to ask about. A unit can want a system, but if it was used three times in six months, that is a material fact in the renewal decision — and one nobody currently has to hand.
107	Tier | Trigger | Review depth
108	Light | No athlete data; single unit; low or one-time cost | Gate features only (Compliance, Privacy, Ownership, Transparency, Interoperability)
109	Standard | Performance data, multi-team use, or recurring cost | Full scorecard
110	Elevated | Physiologic or health data; external data sharing; third-party or AI processing of athlete data | Full scorecard, plus data protection review and Health & Wellness / medical sign-off
111	Status of this appendix
112	These are questions the department needs answers to, and a first attempt at those answers. They are offered as recommendations for the group to discuss — not as adopted positions. Items marked "Recommendation" require ratification, and several need legal, compliance, and medical input before they can be settled.
113	Category | Definition | Examples
114	Performance data | External data generated by the athlete | GPS and player tracking, velocity, force plate output, box-score derivatives
115	Physiologic data | Internal data generated by the athlete | Sleep, heart rate, hydration, body composition, bloodwork
116	Business operations data | Data not generated by athletic performance | Ticket sales, attendance, social following, donor and fan engagement
117	# | Open decision | Who decides
118	1 | Dollar thresholds separating Light / Standard / Elevated review tiers | Business Office
119	2 | Named approver at each control point — who signs at the Business Office, who signs at ITS | Administration / ITS
120	3 | Consent mechanism and system of record for physiologic data | Compliance, Legal, Health & Wellness
121	4 | Whether coaching access to raw physiologic data is restricted, and by what rule | Health & Wellness, Administration
122	5 | Target service-level times for standard and expedited requests | ITS and Administration
123	6 | Where the software inventory register lives and who maintains it | Administration / ITS
124	7 | Whether this is issued as best-practice guidance or as departmental policy | Administration
125	8 | Whether an existing ticketing system can carry the request tracker | ITS

8.2  Product trials and pilots
Trials run under provisional approval in a contained environment:
A defined start and hard end date, agreed at approval.
No physiologic data and no identifiable athlete data until full approval.
A named owner and a stated question the trial is meant to answer.
A mandatory review at the end of the trial that converts to full approval or terminates. A trial that continues has become a purchase without a decision.
9. Workflow
Appendix A  ·  Data categorization, ownership and protection
A1.  How are we categorizing data?
Before ownership can be determined, data has to be sorted into buckets. Three categories, distinguished by who generates the data and whether it is internal or external to the athlete:
A further distinction applies within performance data: individual versus team. Team data is aggregated from individual data and treated as such.
A2.  Who owns the data?
The prevailing position, and the one most commonly stated across the industry, is that data generated by the athlete belongs to the athlete and is held under institutional stewardship. Business operations data is institutional. The boundary is genuinely contestable at the margins — athletes generate a third-down conversion rate, but it is plainly institutional — which is precisely why the categories in A1 matter more than a single ownership statement.
A3.  Does consent work the same way for every category?
Recommendation for discussion. Performance data may reasonably be covered by a blanket consent obtained at onboarding. Physiologic data may warrant consent tied to a specific use and a specific time, rather than a blanket permission — recording what was consented to, for what purpose, and when. The mechanism and system of record for this do not currently exist and would need to be built.
A4.  Who should be able to see raw physiologic data?
Recommendation for discussion. Two related proposals:
No single individual should be the sole holder of athletes' physiologic data, and medical staff should be part of the routing path.
Coaching staff may be better served by summary output than by raw physiologic data — the precedent already exists in how DEXA and body composition results are handled today.
Framing matters here, and this will not be universally welcomed. The intent is to unburden coaches from information that will not change their decisions and to let the specialist own the interpretation — not to withhold. Where that framing fails, the underlying issue is usually trust between staff groups, which a policy document cannot resolve on its own.
A5.  What happens when someone outside Baylor needs access?
External consultants and contractors working with student-athlete data require an executed agreement carrying institutional privacy and data protection terms before access is granted — beyond the standard outside-consultant agreement handled through compliance. This is already current practice and should be stated in the framework so it is applied consistently rather than on a case-by-case basis.
Sharing an individual athlete's data externally — for example, providing performance numbers to a professional scout — requires that athlete's consent.
A6.  What legal considerations sit behind this?
Flagged for legal review, not offered as legal advice:
FERPA protects student records and may impose consent, retention and disclosure obligations when records are released to third parties — including AI vendors that analyze athlete data.
HIPAA governs the use, security, and disclosure of protected health information when tools access medical and injury records.
State privacy laws increasingly scrutinize wearable-derived data such as heart rate, sleep, and stress indicators.
The practical consequence of this framework is that the data category declared at intake determines which of these are in play, which is why the declaration sits on the request form rather than being discovered later.
A7.  What must a request declare about data?
Every request declares: the data category; whether data leaves Baylor systems; who receives and interfaces with the output; where the data is stored; and what happens to it at end of term. These determine the review tier, route the request to the correct reviewers, and let ITS reach a yes-or-no decision faster.
Appendix B  ·  Open decisions for the group
These belong to the stakeholder group, not to Applied Performance. They are the deliberate 20% left open in this draft.
Appendix C  ·  Source materials
NCAA Sports Science Institute — guidance on the Responsible Use of Performance Technologies in College Athletics.
Eversheds Sutherland — “How to get ahead? Harnessing athlete performance data” (summarises the NCAA guidance and the FERPA / HIPAA / state-law considerations above).
Sports Tech Research Network — Quality Framework for Sports Technologies (white paper, assessment sheet, and “Bringing the Framework to Life”, v1.0 December 2024). Basis for the evaluation scorecard.
Baylor Applied Performance — Sports Tech Evaluation Assessment Sheet (2024), the existing internal adaptation of the STRN framework.
Status | DRAFT v0.9 — for discussion, 2026-08-10
Prepared by | Eric Rash, Director of Applied Performance
Requested by | Kenny Boyd
For review | Monday 10 August 2026
Purpose of draft | 80% draft. Decisions reserved for the stakeholder group are marked throughout and collected in Appendix B.
How to read this draft
This document is intentionally unfinished. The process in Sections 4–7 is proposed for adoption, with input from legal, compliance, and medical teams to ensure comprehensive review and address concerns.
NCAA SSI recommendation | Where this framework addresses it
Implement written policies that establish standards and procedures and increase transparency. | This document
Educate student-athletes so that consent is informed | Appendix A — consent and categorization
Manage data rights — ownership, storage, access authority, permitted use | Appendix A; Ownership and Privacy gate features on the scorecard
Establish a process for implementing new technologies, applied consistently and cross-disciplinarily | Phase 1 — Proposal, Approval, Purchase
Develop a system for continual improvement | Phase 3 — Product Review and Renewal Decision
Role | Responsibility in this framework
Requesting party
(Head Coach, Admin Unit Director, or DAPP) | Initiates the request. Completes the Idea Form and internal ATH Form, including the data category declaration.
Business Office | First control point. Filters ALL requests before they proceed — budget, contract, and duplication check.
ITS | Second control point. Technical, security, and integration review; confirms the system can be supported.
Director of Applied Performance (DAPP) | Single point of contact and facilitator. Holds the weekly standing meeting with ITS and relays status to project managers and stakeholders.
Assigned Project Manager | Owns delivery of the individual project. May be administrative staff other than DAPP.
Sport Administrator | Signs off on renewal decisions at Phase 3, informed by the usage review.
Health & Wellness / Medical | Reviews requests involving physiologic or health data (Elevated tier).
What the DAPP role is not
The Director of Applied Performance is the single point of contact — not the subject-matter expert for every system, and not the project manager for every project. The role is to keep requests visible and moving, and to make sure the right people are in the conversation. Delivery accountability stays with the assigned project manager and the requesting unit.
Why the review matters
The review is what gives sign-off authority something to ask about. A unit can want a system, but if it was used three times in six months, that is a material fact in the renewal decision — and one nobody currently has to hand.
Tier | Trigger | Review depth
Light | No athlete data; single unit; low or one-time cost | Gate features only (Compliance, Privacy, Ownership, Transparency, Interoperability)
Standard | Performance data, multi-team use, or recurring cost | Full scorecard
Elevated | Physiologic or health data; external data sharing; third-party or AI processing of athlete data | Full scorecard, plus data protection review and Health & Wellness / medical sign-off
Status of this appendix
These are questions the department needs answers to, and a first attempt at those answers. They are offered as recommendations for the group to discuss — not as adopted positions. Items marked "Recommendation" require ratification, and several need legal, compliance, and medical input before they can be settled.
Category | Definition | Examples
Performance data | External data generated by the athlete | GPS and player tracking, velocity, force plate output, box-score derivatives
Physiologic data | Internal data generated by the athlete | Sleep, heart rate, hydration, body composition, bloodwork
Business operations data | Data not generated by athletic performance | Ticket sales, attendance, social following, donor and fan engagement
# | Open decision | Who decides
1 | Dollar thresholds separating Light / Standard / Elevated review tiers | Business Office
2 | Named approver at each control point — who signs at the Business Office, who signs at ITS | Administration / ITS
3 | Consent mechanism and system of record for physiologic data | Compliance, Legal, Health & Wellness
4 | Whether coaching access to raw physiologic data is restricted, and by what rule | Health & Wellness, Administration
5 | Target service-level times for standard and expedited requests | ITS and Administration
6 | Where the software inventory register lives and who maintains it | Administration / ITS
7 | Whether this is issued as best-practice guidance or as departmental policy | Administration
8 | Whether an existing ticketing system can carry the request tracker | ITS
